words.ex: Thanks to digital technology, Aunt Nodira keeps thousands of family photos on a memory card no bigger than a fingernail.
The café owner on our street still plays records on an old analogue turntable and insists they sound warmer than any streaming app.
The new library in Gulistan offers free wi-fi, so students come there after school to do their online research.
Without the satnav on the dashboard, our driver would never have found the little guesthouse in the hills above Zaamin.
My cousin's running watch uses GPS to record exactly where she ran and how far.
Ships far out in the ocean stay in touch with the coast by satellite, even when there is no phone signal for hundreds of kilometres.
A biotechnology start-up in Tashkent is producing medicine inside harmless bacteria grown in huge steel tanks.
Orchard owners near Urgut are planting disease-resistant apricot trees so that fewer harvests are lost.
My sister's new phone uses artificial intelligence to translate street signs and menus the moment she points the camera at them.
Before designing the new school desks, the team studied ergonomics so that pupils could sit comfortably through long lessons.
My wireless headphones connect to my phone by Bluetooth, so there are no cables to get tangled in my bag.
My brother is a real techie: he reads every review and buys each new gadget the week it comes out.
He keeps his smartphone in his pocket wherever he goes and uses it to call, chat, pay and take photos.
Since he drives a taxi all day, Uncle Bahrom wears a hands-free earpiece so he can take calls without holding his phone.
At the entrance of the new sports centre, every member taps a smart ID card on the reader and the barrier opens.
When the lid of my laptop cracked, the keyboard still worked but the screen was useless.
Our school's computer room has thirty desktop computers, each with a big monitor fixed to the table.
Every evening my brothers argue about whose turn it is to play on the games console connected to the TV.
My little sister swipes through picture books on our family's old tablet, pinching the screen to make the animals bigger.
The ticket machine at the station has a touchscreen, so you just tap the name of your stop.
On the long train ride to Urgench, Gulnora takes her e-reader, which holds hundreds of novels and doesn't tire her eyes.
The heavy old box-shaped television was replaced by a thin flat-screen TV that hangs on the living-room wall.
When the internet stopped working, the IT teacher switched the router off and on again, and the whole school was back online.
The concert in the park started half an hour late because of a technical problem with the sound system.
Jamshid is technically still a student, but he spends most of his time running a small delivery start-up.
The new hospital is technologically far ahead of the old clinic, with scanners the doctors had only read about before.
Zulfiya carries a light notebook to her lectures so that she can type her notes as the professor speaks.
Years ago, Diyor listened to music on a tiny MP3 player clipped to his jacket, which held just two hundred songs.
Before the school concert began, the singer tapped the microphone twice to check that the speakers were on.
Our classroom now has an interactive whiteboard, so pupils can drag pictures across it with their fingers.
Rapid technological progress means that even remote mountain villages can now get fast internet.
